summary: Defines two new categories of IP performance metrics: spatial metrics, which measure the performance of parts of a path, and multicast metrics, covering multiple measurement points. They extend the earlier two-point approach.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines IP performance measurements for path segments and groups of destinations. The results can show where delay or loss occurs and how network performance differs among receivers.

questions: how is multicast group delay measured
what is a routers digest in ippm
subtitle: Metrics for measuring individual path segments and the performance seen by a group of receivers.

tldr.problem: End-to-end measurements between two points cannot show where along a path delay or packet loss occurs or how a group of receivers is served.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines spatial vectors and segment samples, plus one-to-group vectors and statistics for delay, loss, and delay variation.
tldr.outcome: The metrics extend IPPM measurements to multiple observation points and receiver groups. RFC 5644 is updated by RFC 6248.

today: RFC 5644 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 2009, and is updated by RFC 6248. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Extending End-to-End Measurements
sections.content:
Earlier IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) measured performance between two endpoints. RFC 5644 adds spatial metrics for points along a source-to-destination path and one-to-group metrics for one source and multiple destinations.

The metrics derive from one-way end-to-end measurements and use packets dedicated to testing, called active measurement. Passive measurement of ordinary user traffic, as well as group-to-one and group-to-group topologies, is outside the RFC's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: End-to-end measurements show the result between two endpoints. These metrics add observations along a path and at multiple destinations.

sections.title: Points of Interest, Vectors, and Matrices
sections.content:
A point of interest is a host that collects measurements. For spatial metrics, these points are selected routers on the path, called the routers digest. For one-to-group metrics, they are the destination hosts.

A vector collects results for one source packet as it is observed at several points. A matrix combines vectors from several packets, organizing the measurements across both the path or receiver group and time. A reference point is the server where statistical calculations are performed.
sections.plainLanguage: A vector records one test packet at several measurement points. A matrix combines those vectors to show results across locations and time.

sections.title: Spatial Vectors and Segment Samples
sections.content:
The RFC defines spatial vectors for one-way delay, packet loss, and IP packet delay variation. A delay vector records when a test packet reaches each selected router and the destination. A loss vector records whether each router observed the packet.

Segment samples compare observations at two routers. The RFC defines samples for segment delay and packet loss, plus two delay-variation forms: one compares successive packets, while the other compares values with the minimum delay. Measurements may appear inconsistent when clocks differ, routes change, or a collection point cannot observe a packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Spatial vectors record a test packet at selected routers. Comparing observations at two routers estimates delay or loss on the segment between them.

sections.title: One-to-Group Measurements
sections.content:
One-to-group vectors collect one-way delay, packet-loss, or delay-variation results for a packet sent from one source to multiple receivers. The group identifier is optional, so the metrics also apply when there is only one receiver.

When used for one-to-one measurement, these metrics give the same results as the corresponding one-to-one metrics. For a group, the vectors provide individual receiver results that can be summarized with group statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: One-to-group vectors record how the same source packet reaches each destination. The same definitions also work when the measurement has one receiver.

sections.title: Statistics Across Receivers
sections.content:
The RFC defines group summaries for delay, packet loss, and delay variation. Delay statistics include each receiver's mean, the group mean, the range of receiver means, and the maximum receiver mean. Loss statistics include individual receiver loss ratios, the overall group ratio, a comparative ratio, and the range across receivers.

Group delay variation is the range between receivers' delay-variation values. The usual value uses the 1-10^(-3) quantile of delay above the minimum; the RFC also suggests 1-10^-5 for more demanding services. The chosen quantile should be reported.
sections.plainLanguage: Group statistics summarize each receiver's results and differences across the group. Reporting both the range and its minimum and maximum helps explain how receivers compare.

sections.title: Reporting, Scale, and Security
sections.content:
Collecting results from many measurement points can consume storage, bandwidth, and processing capacity. Points of interest can send raw samples for centralized calculation or send summary statistics. Summaries reduce traffic but may hide patterns such as which packets were lost; the RFC defines its metrics using statistics computed over time before combining results across points.

Spatial reports MUST list points of interest in path order and include timestamp uncertainty. Reports should also describe the path, group size, and measurement method where applicable. False reports, spoofed measurement points, and excessive reporting can mislead traffic engineering or overload a reference point, so the RFC recommends protecting reports and controlling test rates.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending every measurement can overload the collection point, while summaries can hide detail. Reports should include enough context to interpret them and should be protected from false or excessive traffic.
